title: Repeater operation, tones and Q signals
blurb: Use reverse, CTCSS, DTMF and DMR settings, solve common access problems, and read the common Q signals.

T2B01.why: **Reverse** swaps receive and transmit so you can **listen on the repeater's input**.
T2B01.trap: It doesn't change power or listen to the output, which is normal.

T2B02.why: **CTCSS** is a sub-audible tone sent with voice to open a receiver's squelch.
T2B02.trap: DTMF is audible touch-tone, and tone burst is a short audible tone.

T2B03.why: In a **linked network**, what one repeater receives is transmitted by all repeaters in the network.

T2B04.why: A wrong **offset**, **CTCSS tone** or **DCS code** can each block access even if you hear the output. All are possible.

T2B05.why: Audio that drops out on peaks means **talking too loudly**: you over-deviate your FM signal.
T2B05.trap: Too little deviation makes you quiet, not choppy.

T2B06.why: **DTMF** sends **two simultaneous audio tones** per key.
T2B06.trap: CTCSS is a single sub-audible tone.

T2B07.why: Join a talkgroup by **programming its ID into your radio**.
T2B07.trap: Joining is a radio setting, not a registration with a coordinator or control operator.

T2B08.why: Interfering stations should **negotiate** continued use. Arriving first confers no right.

T2B09.why: Simplex channels let stations **within range talk directly without tying up a repeater**.

T2B10.trap: QRN is natural noise like static, and QSB is fading.

T2B11.trap: QSL means message received, and QRZ asks who is calling.

T2B12.why: The DMR **color code** is an access code programmed into your radio for a specific repeater.
T2B12.trap: It doesn't set the offset, identify the codec or report health.

T2B13.why: **Squelch** mutes the receiver audio when no signal is present.
T2B13.trap: It isn't noise blanking for impulse noise.

T2B14.why: A **talkgroup** is a DMR identifier that organizes traffic, so you hear only the groups you want.
